title.en: The Creation: Sky Woman, Turtle Bearer, and the Twin Spirits
title.zh: 創世：天女、負地之龜與雙靈

region.en: The floating island in the cloud sea (symbolic pin above the Seneca country)
region.zh: 雲海中的浮島（象徵性定位於塞內卡之地上空）

texts.period: Collected by Harriet Maxwell Converse over 22 years among the Seneca, ed. A. C. Parker (1908)

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (NY State Museum Bulletin 125, 1908), 'Creation'

summary.en: By Iroquois mythology the earth was the thought of the Indian Ruler of a great island which floats in space. When the Great Ruler bade the council tree be uprooted and bade the pregnant Sky Woman look down, he wrapped around her a great ray of light and sent her down to the cloud sea. The animals counseled in alarm: the Beaver dived and never returned, the Duck floated dead, until the Muskrat - knowing the way - brought up a portion of the oeh-da (earth) in his paw. The Turtle bore it on his hard shell and became the Earth Bearer; when he stirs, the seas rise in great waves, and when restless and violent, earthquakes yawn and devour. On the island the Sky Woman bore twin lives - one peaceful, one restless and vicious, the latter thrusting himself through under his mother's arm - and Hah-gweh-di-yu, Spirit of Good, shaped the sky with the palm of his hand, creating the Sun from his dead mother's face, the Moon and Stars from her breast, giving the Earth her body as Great Mother; while Hah-gweh-da-et-gah set Darkness in the west sky, sundered the mountains, gnarled the forests, and led monsters to the sea. When the Good Mind had pulled up the tree of light he beheld his face in the pool beneath and, molding images in red clay, transformed them into living beings: thus did the human race take origin.
summary.zh: 易洛魁神話說：大地原是至高主宰對一座浮於太空的巨島的意念。主宰命拔起議事樹，令懷孕的天女俯視深淵，以光包裹她，送她降向雲海。眾獸驚慌聚議：河狸潛水不返，鴨浮屍而上，直至識途的麝鼠以爪捧上一撮「奧達」（土）。龜以硬殼負之，成為「負地者」——牠一動，海起巨浪；牠暴怒翻騰，地震裂谷。島上，天女生下雙生——一者安寧，一者暴躁邪惡（自母腋下硬擠而出）；善靈哈格威迪尤以掌成天，自亡母之面造太陽、自其胸造月與星，把大地認作大母親；惡靈則在西方天際布下黑暗，裂山毀林、縱獸入海。善靈拔起光之樹後，於樹下水池中照見己容，遂以紅黏土捏像而賦生——人類由此起源。

sensitivity.note: Converse/Parker 1908; public domain. Parker annotates the moral-dualism evolution from Ioskeha/Tawiscara (1636) to the Good and Evil Minds.

passages.text: In the far away days of this floating island there grew one stately tree that branched beyond the range of vision. Perpetually laden with fruit and blossoms, the air was fragrant with its perfume, and the people gathered to its shade where councils were held. One day the Great Ruler said to his people: 'We will make a new place where another people may grow. Under our council tree is a great cloud sea which calls for our help. It is lonesome. It knows no rest and calls for light. We will talk to it. The roots of our council tree point to it and will show the way.' Having commanded that the tree be uprooted, the Great Ruler peered into the depths where the roots had guided, and summoning Ata-en-sic, who was with child, bade her look down. Ata-en-sic saw nothing, but the Great Ruler knew that the sea voice was calling, and bidding her carry its life, wrapped around her a great ray of light and sent her down to the cloud sea.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 32-33; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Dazzled by the descending light enveloping Ata-en-sic, there was great consternation among the animals and birds inhabiting the cloud sea, and they counseled in alarm. 'If it falls it may destroy us,' they cried. 'Where can it rest?' asked the Duck. 'Only the oeh-da (earth) can hold it,' said the Beaver, 'the oeh-da which lies at the bottom of our waters, and I will bring it.' The Beaver went down but never returned. Then the Duck ventured, but soon its dead body floated to the surface. Many of the divers had tried and failed when the Muskrat, knowing the way, volunteered to obtain it and soon returned bearing a small portion in his paw. 'But it is heavy,' said he, 'and will grow fast. Who will bear it?' The Turtle was willing, and the oeh-da was placed on his hard shell. Having received a resting place for the light, the water birds, guided by its glow, flew upward, and receiving the woman on their widespread wings, bore her down to the Turtle's back. And Hah-nu-nah, the Turtle, became the Earth Bearer. When he stirs, the seas rise in great waves, and when restless and violent, earthquakes yawn and devour.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 33; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: To her solitude two lives were coming, one peaceful and patient, the other restless and vicious. The latter, discovering light under his mother's arm, thrust himself through, to contentions and strife, the right born entered life for freedom and peace. These were the Do-ya-da-no, the twin brothers, Spirits of Good and Evil. At the birth of Hah-gweh-di-yu his Sky Mother, Ata-en-sic, had died, and the island was still dim in the dawn of its new life when, grieving at his mother's death, he shaped the sky with the palm of his hand, and creating the Sun from her face, lifted it there, saying, 'You shall rule here where your face will shine forever.' But Hah-gweh-da-et-gah set Darkness in the west sky, to drive the Sun down behind it. Hah-gweh-di-yu then drew forth from the breast of his Mother, the Moon and the Stars, and led them to the Sun as his sisters who would guard his night sky. He gave to the Earth her body, its Great Mother, from whom was to spring all life.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 33-34; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: When the earth was completed and Hah-gweh-di-yu had bestowed a protecting Spirit upon each of his creation, he besought Hah-gweh-da-et-gah to reconcile his vicious existences to the peacefulness of his own, but Hah-gweh-da-et-gah refused, and challenged Hah-gweh-di-yu to combat, the victor to become the ruler of the earth. Hah-gweh-da-et-gah proposed weapons which he could control, poisonous roots strong as flint, monster's teeth, and fangs of serpents. But these Hah-gweh-di-yu refused, selecting the thorns of the giant crab-apple tree, which were arrow pointed and strong. With the thorns they fought. The battle continued many days, ending in the overthrow of Hah-gweh-da-et-gah. Hah-gweh-di-yu, having now become the ruler, banished his brother to a pit under the earth, whence he can not return. The first beings of earth were a race of gods who returned to the sky world when the Good Mind created men-beings. After the Good Mind had pulled up the tree of light he beheld his face in the pool of water in which it had grown. This gave him the idea of molding images in red clay which he afterward transformed into living beings. Thus did the human race take origin.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 36 and footnote; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Naming the Winds: Bear, Panther, Moose, and Fawn
title.zh: 為四方之風命名：熊、豹、麋與幼鹿

region.en: Ga-oh's lodge in the north sky, and the four gates of the sky
region.zh: 北天風神之居與天的四門

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Naming the Winds'

summary.en: When, in the creation of the earth, Hah-gweh-di-yu limited the duties of the powerful Ga-oh to the sky, assigning to him the governing of the tempests, he blew a strong blast that shook the whole earth to trembling, and summoned his assistants to a council. Ga-oh chose his aids from the terrestrial because of their knowledge of the earth: the bulky Bear Ya-o-gah, who had battled the boisterous winds as he came pushing mountains from his path, is bound and leashed into the north sky - 'you can freeze the waters with your cold breath; in your broad arms you can carry the wild tempests... You shall be North Wind'; the gentle Fawn Ne-o-ga walks with the summer sun and rules the flock of summer winds in the south; the ugly, fierce Panther Da-jo-ji, with a sound as of great claws tearing the heavens into rifts, carries the whirlwind on his strong back and is leashed to the west, 'where even the Sun will hurry to hide when you howl your warning to the night'; and the Moose O-yan-do-ne, whose horns spread wide to push back the forests and whose breath blows the mist and leads the cold rains, takes the east. Thus, with his assistants, does Ga-oh control his storms. When the north wind blows strong, the Iroquois say, 'The Bear is prowling in the sky.'
summary.zh: 創世之時，善靈把風神加奧的力量限定於天界，令其執掌風暴。加奧轟然一嘯，大地震顫，召集助手議事——他選擇地上的獸，因其識得大地：笨重的熊亞奧加一路推開群山而來，被縛上北天的韁繩——「你能以寒息凍結水面；你能以巨臂擁抱狂飆……你就是北風」；溫柔的幼鹿內奧加與夏日同行，執掌南天的夏日風群；兇惡的黑豹達喬吉撕天裂雲而至，背負旋風，被縛往西天——「你一長嘯，連太陽也要急急躲藏」；麋鹿奧揚多內角闊如犁、氣息引雨，領東方之風。自此四風各司其方：北風起時，易洛魁人便說「熊在天上巡行」。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. The four winds as four beast-wardens is the Iroquois signature of the cardinal-direction myth.

passages.text: When, in the creation of the earth, Hah-gweh-di-yu limited the duties of the powerful Ga-oh to the sky, assigning to him the governing of the tempests, he blew a strong blast that shook the whole earth to trembling, and summoned his assistants to a council. Ga-oh chose his aids from the terrestrial because of their knowledge of the earth; and when his reverberating call had ceased its thunderous echoes, he opened his north gate wide across the sky and called Ya-o-gah, the Bear. Lumbering over the mountains as he pushed them from his path, Ya-o-gah, the bulky bear, who had battled the boisterous winds as he came, took his place at Ga-oh's gate and waited the mission of his call. Said Ga-oh, 'Ya-o-gah, you are strong, you can freeze the waters with your cold breath; in your broad arms you can carry the wild tempests, and clasp the whole earth when I bid you destroy. I will place you in my far north, there to watch the herd of my winter winds when I loose them in the sky. You shall be North Wind. Enter your home.' And the bear lowered his head for the leash with which Ga-oh bound him, and submissively took his place in the north sky.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 38; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: In a gentler voice Ga-oh called Ne-o-ga, the Fawn, and a soft breeze as of the summer crept over the sky; the air grew fragrant with the odor of flowers, and there were voices as of babbling brooks telling the secrets of the summer to the tune of birds, as Ne-o-ga came proudly lifting her head. Said Ga-oh, 'You walk with the summer sun, and know all its paths; you are gentle, and kind as the sunbeam, and will rule my flock of the summer winds in peace. You shall be the South Wind. Bend your head while I leash you to the sky, for you are swift, and might return from me to the earth.' And the gentle fawn followed Ga-oh to his great gate which opens the south sky.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 38-39; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Again Ga-oh trumpeted a shrill blast, and all the sky seemed threatening; an ugly darkness crept into the clouds that sent them whirling in circles of confusion; a quarrelsome, shrieking voice snarled through the air, and with a sound as of great claws tearing the heavens into rifts, Da-jo-ji, the Panther, sprang to the gate. Said Ga-oh, 'You are ugly, and fierce, and can fight the strong storms; you can climb the high mountains, and tear down the forests; you can carry the whirlwind on your strong back, and toss the great sea waves high in the air, and snarl at the tempests if they stray from my gate. You shall be the West Wind. Go to the west sky, where even the Sun will hurry to hide when you howl your warning to the night.' And Da-jo-ji, dragging his leash as he stealthily crept along, followed Ga-oh to the furthermost west sky.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 39; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Yet Ga-oh rested not. The earth was flat, and in each of its four corners he must have an assistant. One corner yet remained, and again Ga-oh's strong blast shook the earth. And there arose a moan like the calling of a lost mate, the sky shivered in a cold rain, the whole earth clouded in mist, a crackling sound as of great horns crashing through the forest trees dinned the air, and O-yan-do-ne, the Moose, stood stamping his hoofs at the gate. Said Ga-oh, as he strung a strong leash around his neck, 'Your breath blows the mist, and can lead the cold rains; your horns spread wide, and can push back the forests to widen the path for my storms as with your swift hoofs you race with my winds. You shall be the East Wind, and blow your breath to chill the young clouds as they float through the sky.' Thus, with his assistants, does Ga-oh control his storms. When the north wind blows strong, the Iroquois say, 'The Bear is prowling in the sky'; if the west wind is violent, 'The Panther is whining.' When the east wind chills with its rain, 'The Moose is spreading his breath'; and when the south wind wafts soft breezes, 'The Fawn is returning to its Doe.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 39; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: He-no, the Thunderer: The Niagara Serpent and the Horseshoe Fall
title.zh: 雷神希農：尼亞加拉巨蛇與馬蹄瀑

region.en: Behind the great falls at Niagara

texts.period: Converse (1908), with Esquire Johnson's account recorded 1876

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'He-no, the Thunderer'

summary.en: As guardian of the heavens, He-no is intrusted with the thunder, the voice of admonition, which can be heard above the turmoil of the tempests; it is also his duty to direct the rain for refreshing the earth. As a human being he wears in his hair a magic feather which renders him invulnerable to the attacks of Evil. In his celestial travels He-no carries on his back a great basket containing boulders of the chert rock, which he hurls at evil spirits whenever he discovers them in the sky; sometimes the evil spirits evade these boulders and they fall to the earth enveloped in fire. Before He-no was transferred to the skies, he dwelt behind the great falls at Niagara, where he controlled the roaring of its waters. 'I can wash the world if you want me to,' he told God, in Esquire Johnson's telling. During his terrestrial life the Iroquois were terrified by the annual visits of a hideous serpent that lived in a cave near the Niagara cataract: toward the spring this creature would emerge, enter the burial places of the Iroquois, feed on the dead, and poison the land with pestilence. He-no pursued it, and overtaking it as it wound through Buffalo creek threw a terrific thunderbolt upon it; in its writhings the monster pushed the shores of the creek into the bends which yet remain. Slowly dying, it floated down the Niagara river to the verge of the great cataract where, in a final death throe, its bulky body arched backward in a semicircle extending from shore to shore; the dead body restrained the rushing waters for a time, but finding an opening through the rocks they dashed on, sundering the ledge - and thus was formed the Horse Shoe fall of the great cataract.
summary.zh: 作為天界守護者，希農執掌雷霆——高過風暴喧囂的警世之聲；他亦司降雨潤土。他化人形時髮間插著一根使其不受邪惡所傷的魔法羽毛。他在天上行旅時背負巨筐，內裝燧石巨礫，見邪靈在天空出現便擲石擊之；邪靈偶或閃避，石塊裹火墜地。希農上天之前住在尼亞加拉大瀑之後，掌管瀑聲。老酋約翰遜的講述裡，他對神說：「若你願意，我能洗淨整個世界。」他尚在人間時，一條棲於瀑旁岩洞的醜蛇年年為患：春水初漲，此物出洞鑽入易洛魁人的墓地吞食死者，歸途毒化大地，疫病流行。希農追之，在水牛溪畔以巨雷擊中；怪物掙扎間把溪岸擠出至今猶存的河曲。它垂死順尼亞加拉河漂向瀑口，最後的掙扎使龐軀向後彎成跨岸的半環；屍身一度攔住奔流，水自岩隙破峽而出，掀翻岩棚——馬蹄瀑由此而成。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. The Thunderer hates witches, underwater people and False Faces - he must be soothed with tobacco incense.

passages.text: As guardian of the heavens, He-no is intrusted with the thunder, the voice of admonition, which can be heard above the turmoil of the tempests. It is also his duty to direct the rain for refreshing the earth. In the planting season, He-no has supervision of the seeds, and in the growing time renders beneficent aid in ripening the fruits and maturing the harvest. He-no can assume the form of a human being and, as such, dressed as a warrior, he wears in his hair a magic feather, which renders him invulnerable to the attacks of Evil. On these occasions he is invested with authority to inflict dire punishment upon evil doers, and is dreaded as the avenger of vice. In his celestial travels, He-no carries on his back a great basket containing boulders of the chert rock, which he hurls at evil spirits whenever he discovers them in the sky. Sometimes the evil spirits evade these boulders and they fall to the earth enveloped in fire.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 39-40; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Sometime afterward God met a man walking about by himself and addressing him in a pleasant way, asked him what he was looking for. He said he was amusing himself looking around the world, that he had a great many grandchildren not far off, that he was in fact the Thunderer and had many grandchildren near and loved them much. Moreover, that he wished to be set about some great work and asked God to give him something to do. God said to him, 'What can you do?' He said, 'I can wash the world if you want me to.' 'Very well,' said God, 'that would be a good work for you to do and I will employ you to do that work for me. You can make it rain and wash the earth often.' (Taken verbatim from the manuscript notes of Mrs Asher Wright, a missionary who interviewed Johnson in 1876.)
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, footnote; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: During the terrestrial life of He-no, the Iroquois people were terrified by the annual visits of a hideous serpent that lived in a cave near the Niagara cataract. Toward the spring, when the rivers were loosing themselves and pouring their torrents into Lake Erie, this creature would emerge from its cave, and entering the burial places of the Iroquois, feed on the dead; and in the sinuous paths of its return, would poison the land with a pestilence to which large numbers of the people fell victims.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 42-43; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: He-no pursued it, and overtaking it as it wound through the De-gi-ya-goh (Buffalo creek) threw a terrific thunderbolt upon it, and in its writhings to escape, the monster pushed the shores of the creek into the bends which yet remain. Slowly dying, it floated down the Niagara river to the verge of the great cataract where, in a final death throe, its bulky body arched backward in a semicircle extending from shore to shore. The dead body restrained the rushing waters for a time, but finding an opening through the rocks, they dashed on, sundering the ledge which shelved over the river as they tumbled down the abyss in a riotous roar. And thus was formed the Horse Shoe fall of the great cataract.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 42-43; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Gun-no-do-yah, the Thunder Boy, and the Human Snake
title.zh: 雷童貢諾多亞與人形蛇

region.en: Lake Ontario and the Thunderers' sky
region.zh: 安大略湖與雷族的天空

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Gun-no-do-yah, the Thunder Boy, and the Human Snake'

summary.en: He-no had hurled down a terrific rain storm which had flooded the land and overflowed the lakes and rivers, and, in pity for Earth, sent down one of his aids to pacify the waters. Passing over a canton of the Senecas he heard a voice wailing in great distress, and descending found a small child floating in the flood that had carried its parents away. Recognizing the child as Gun-no-do-yah, the son of a chief, he determined to save it, and carrying it to his home in the sky laid it to rest on a strong black cloud. He-no, who had been out drilling his Thunderers, upon returning overheard the boy grieving the loss of his parents and, deciding to adopt him, transformed him into a Thunder Hunter: 'There dwells in a lake a human monster that no mortal has been able to kill; my Thunderers, not being of earth, have sought him in vain... Gun-no-do-yah, having been human, can follow the trails of the earth.' For many months the hunt was in vain until, under the black clouds of Lake Ontario, the monster beckoned him to come closer: 'I know your strong arrows; they can not reach me. He-no, your master, I fear not; I scorn his thunder... Come with me. I will guide you to my home in the rocks deep below which the sun never sees. Come and comb my long mane, it is tangled with fish and is heavy.' As Gun-no-do-yah drew his bow with all his strength the string snapped; seizing him in its hissing mouth the monster carried him down to the bottom of the lake. He-no was sleeping when the boy appeared to him in a dream; the Thunderers ploughed through the deep caves under the water, found the monster sleeping, drew it from its hiding place and carried it to He-no, who slew it and drew from its body the life of Gun-no-do-yah. Lake Ontario is noted for its violent winds, and when they drive the canoe high on the waves, the Indians know that the spirit of the snake is there 'twisting the water' in its revenge; and when the lightning darts quick across the sky, they whisper in awe, 'Gun-no-do-yah is chasing it!'
summary.zh: 希農擲下暴雨，大水泛濫成災；他憐惜大地，遣一名助手下凡安撫洪水。助手飛過塞內卡人的村社時，聽見哭喊，降落水面，發現一個漂在洪水中的孩子——他的父母已被水沖走。這正是酋長之子貢諾多亞；助手把孩子抱上雲端安放於黑雲之上。希農聽聞男孩哀悼雙親，決定收養他，把他變成「雷獵手」：「湖中住著一個人形怪物，凡人殺之不得；我的雷族非地上之身，遍尋無果……貢諾多亞曾是凡人，能踏地上的蹤跡。」數月無功。一個烏雲壓湖之夜，怪物喚他近前：「我認得你的神箭，但箭到不了我身；我不怕你的主子，我鄙視他的雷霆……來吧，我領你去我太陽照不到的深岩之家。來替我梳理長鬣——裡面纏滿魚，重得很。」貢諾多亞張弓用力，弓弦啪然崩斷；怪物張開嘶嘶的大口把他拖入湖底。希農在夢中聽他陳情，大怒，遣最勇的雷戰士犁遍水下深穴，把熟睡的怪物拖出，殺之，自其軀中取出貢諾多亞的性命。安大略湖以狂風著稱——風把獨木舟掀上浪尖時，印第安人知道那是蛇靈在「攪水」復仇；閃電疾掠長空時，他們便敬畏地低語：「貢諾多亞在追牠！」

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. The underwater people (Jo-di'kwa-do') are great sorcerers; their daughters especially beautiful - landmen who don the shining snake-skin suits become forever horned serpents.

passages.text: He-no, the Thunderer, had hurled down a terrific rain storm which had flooded the land and overflowed the lakes and rivers, and, in pity for Earth, sent down Ha-de-ne-no-da-on, one of his aids, to pacify the waters. As Ha-de-ne-no-da-on was passing over a canton of the Senecas, he heard a voice wailing in great distress, and descending, found a small child floating in the flood that had carried its parents away. Recognizing the child as Gun-no-do-yah, the son of a chief whom on his earth visits he had frequently seen, and who was a great warrior, he determined to save it, and carrying it to his home in the sky, laid it to rest on a strong black cloud and returned to earth on his peace mission. He-no, who had been out drilling his Thunderers, upon returning overheard the boy grieving the loss of his parents and, deciding to adopt him, transformed him into a Thunder Hunter.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 42-43; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Said He-no, 'He has been sent to me; he is a human and knows all the paths of the earth, and can render me great service. There dwells in a lake a human monster that no mortal has been able to kill; my Thunderers, not being of earth, have sought him in vain; and he defies me and my thunderbolts while he ravages the lake of its fish, and frightening the fishers away deprives the people of their food. Gun-no-do-yah, having been human, can follow the trails of the earth. I will make him powerful, and give him a strong bow and arrow, and he shall follow my storms when my black clouds shadow the lakes, and hunt the monster to its death.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 43; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: But one night when the Thunderers were savagely hurling their bolts over the lake which the clouds obscured in their blackness, and the fish swam deep in fear of the reverberating echoes, Gun-no-do-yah went boldly into the lake, and encountering the snake again drew his bow, when the snake beckoned to him to come closer and listen; and then it began to speak. 'Come closer,' it said, 'and fear me not. I know you well, and I know your strong arrows; they can not reach me. He-no, your master, I fear not; I scorn his thunder, the lightning passes by me. Your task is useless and you need not serve him. I am your friend and will teach you how to shoot the fish in the night. I will reveal to you all the secrets of the waters. Come with me. I will guide you to my home in the rocks deep below which the sun never sees. Come and comb my long mane, it is tangled with fish and is heavy.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 43-44; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Gun-no-do-yah would not listen, he came to kill; but as he drew his bow with all his strength, the string snapped, the dead arrow fell to the water, and he was powerless. Raising its head high in the air, the monster opened its hissing mouth, and seizing Gun-no-do-yah, carried him down to the bottom of the lake. He-no was sleeping, when Gun-no-do-yah appeared to him in a dream and related his misfortune... Diligently they ploughed through the deep caves under the water, where they found the monster sleeping; and drawing it from its hiding place carried it to He-no, who slew it and drew from its body the life giving Gun-no-do-yah. And great was the rejoicing of the Thunderers and warriors. Now, that Gun-no-do-yah had been saved, He-no would never permit him to revisit the earth... Lake Ontario is noted for its violent winds, and when they drive the canoe high on the waves, the Indians know that the spirit of the snake is there 'twisting the water' in its revenge and when the lightning darts quick across the sky, they whisper in awe, 'Gun-no-do-yah is chasing it!'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 44-45; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: O-se-ha-da-gaar, the Dew Eagle: The Lake of Dew on His Back
title.zh: 露鷹奧塞哈達加爾：背上的露水之湖

region.en: Lodge far beyond the west sky

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'O-se-ha-da-gaar, the Dew Eagle'

summary.en: In the myth lore of the Iroquois, where everything animate or inanimate is endowed with supernatural powers, the myths relating to the sun have special significance. But there are Spirits of Evil who roam the Earth and defying the Sun seek to overthrow its beneficent power: the Fire Spirit may summon his Flame Bearers and, descending to Earth, burn and destroy the harvests. At the coming of the Fire Spirit, mountains shrink down, the thirsting valleys suck dry the streams and springs, night pales her stars, and all Earth faints. In vain Ga-oh searches the heavens for his hiding winds; in vain He-no hunts his thunderbolts to hurl at the Flame Bearers. But to this desolation comes O-se-ha-da-gaar, a great bird whose lodge is far beyond the west sky and who carries a lake of dew in the hollow of its back, faithfully guarded by a band of Listeners, great birds who fly far above the Sun, hear every sound and know every voice in the heavens. When the Fire Spirit suffocates the Earth, they speed to her voice and bear it to the Dew Eagle, who hears, and pluming for flight pushes the skies far apart, obscuring the Sun with his vast spreading wings as they dip to the east and the west fanning gentle breezes, and mist veils the skies as through his fluttering wings he sifts down from his lake the dews to refresh the famishing Earth. Then all nature revives, the Fire Spirit flees, and her harvests rise to new life.
summary.zh: 易洛魁神話中萬物皆有靈性，而關於太陽的神話尤具深意。但也有邪靈在地上橫行、公然挑戰太陽的恩澤——火靈可召其火焰使者下凡焚燬莊稼。火靈一至，山嶽萎縮，乾渴的谷地把溪泉吸盡，夜色掩星，大地昏厥。風神遍尋不見藏匿的風，雷神遍尋不見可擲的雷石，一切似已無望。此時，露鷹奧塞哈達加爾自西天之外的巢居而來——牠背上馱著一泓露水之湖；一群「傾聽者」巨鳥飛翔在太陽之上，聽盡天上的聲音。火靈窒息大地時，眾鳥把她的呼聲送到露鷹耳中；鷹展翅高飛，把天穹推向兩旁，雙翼遮日、自東而西扇起微風；霧靄垂天，牠篩下的露水滋潤飢渴的大地。於是萬物復甦，火靈遁逃，田疇重煥生機。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. Parker notes the Dew Eagle has been stripped of the thunder power other races gave the Thunder Bird - Hi'no took that office, and the Eagle labors faithfully when Hi'no fails to come. A legend says an enormous white eagle from the east ocean will battle with the Dew Eagle until he dies; then the Ongweh'owe will no longer have woods and fields but dry desert places where they will starve.

passages.text: In the myth lore of the Iroquois, where everything animate or inanimate is endowed with supernatural powers either evil or good, the myths relating to the sun, so fecund with life-giving power, have special significance. Although never wandering from his path across the sky, the Sun controls his broad dominion through his assistants. Serving Spirits, whom he endows with various powers and sends down to Earth to fulfil his missions... But there are others, Spirits of Evil, who roam the Earth, and defying the Sun, seek to overthrow its beneficent power. Among these is the Fire Spirit who, malevolently jealous of the Spirits of Good, may summon his Flame Bearers and, descending to Earth, burn and destroy the harvests. At the coming of the Fire Spirit, mountains shrink down, the thirsting valleys suck dry the streams and springs. Night pales her stars, and all Earth faints.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 45-46; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: In vain Ga-oh searches the heavens for his hiding winds. In vain He-no hunts his thunderbolts to hurl at the Flame Bearers, and all seems hopeless and lost. But to this desolation comes O-se-ha-da-gaar, a great bird, whose lodge is far beyond the west sky, and who carries a lake of dew in the hollow of its back. O-se-ha-da-gaar is wise, and does not listen to every call. He knows his power and waits. He is faithfully guarded by a band of Listeners, great birds who fly far above the Sun and can see all that passes below. They hear every sound and know every voice in the heavens, and watch the soft winds which waft the summer clouds to gather the showers; and when the Fire Spirit suffocates the Earth, they speed to her voice, and bear it to O-se-ha-da-gaar who waits in his lodge.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 46-47; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Then O-se-ha-da-gaar hears; and pluming for flight, pushes the skies far apart, obscuring the Sun with his vast spreading wings as they dip to the east and the west fanning gentle breezes, and mist veils the skies as through his fluttering wings he sifts down from his lake the dews to refresh the famishing Earth. Then all nature revives, the Fire Spirit flees; the parching Earth bares her broad breast to the falling dews; her glad rivers and lakes rejoice, and her harvests rise to new life. At the Harvest Feast of the Iroquois, the Creator is thanked for having bestowed upon the people the guarding vigilance of He-no, and is implored not to withdraw from them his power, which controls the gentle rains in the seedtime and the dews in the ripening.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 47; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Sais-tah-go-wa: How the Rainbow Was Made from a Sea Serpent
title.zh: 賽斯托瓦：彩虹由海蛇化成

region.en: The arc of the sky between east and west

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'O-ga-nyo-da and Sais-tah-go-wa, the Rainbow and the Serpent'

summary.en: In the creation of the earth the Sky Woman gave birth to the twins, Hah-gweh-di-yu and Hah-gweh-da-et-gah; and with their birth Good and Evil came upon the Earth, for between the brothers there was continual strife. Hah-gweh-di-yu created beautiful rivers and planted high hills to guard their peaceful flow through the valleys, which enraged Hah-gweh-da-et-gah, who brought forth Sais-tah-go-wa, a sea monster, directing him to enter and destroy them. Accustomed to the freedom of the broad seas, Sais-tah-go-wa was furious when restricted by the banks of the streams, and viciously strove to rend them apart, writhing his way through the waters and hurling great rocks upon them as they fled to the sea. Hastening to their rescue, Hah-gweh-di-yu caused the monster, dreading his power, to seek escape: being unable to return through the rivers he had destroyed, he fled to the sky. The Sun was peacefully tracking its trail across the heavens when Sais-tah-go-wa appeared, and upon learning what the monster had done, determined that it should never return to the earth to injure the creations of Hah-gweh-di-yu, and throwing him across the sky, clasped him down to the east and the west. It chanced at this time that He-no, the Thunderer, was passing on his way through a storm, and admiring the beautiful colors of Sais-tah-go-wa as he stretched across the sky, picked him up, saying, 'My Lightning Hunter needs this for his bow,' and straightway carried him up to his lodge. Sais-tah-go-wa is restless in his captivity, and when He-no is busy directing his storms, endeavors to escape; but the ever watchful Sun detects him, and again bending him across the sky, paints him with his brightest colors that he may be discovered by He-no. In summer showers the red man sees Sais-tah-go-wa in the resplendent hues that arch the sky, and as they fade away and the sun comes forth, he exclaims, 'The rain is past! - Sais-tah-go-wa tried to escape, but He-no has taken him back to his lodge!'
summary.zh: 天女生下雙生兄弟，善惡二靈自此同居於世，鬥爭不休。善靈闢出美麗的河流、植下高山以護其安流，惡靈大怒，遣出海怪賽斯托瓦入河毀壞。慣於遼闊大海的海怪被溪岸所拘，狂怒地扭身撕裂河川、投石阻流。善靈趕來相救；海怪懼其神威，既無法經由自己毀掉的河道返回，便逃往天空。太陽正沿天路安行，見此情景，決不許怪物再回大地傷害善靈的造物，便把他橫拋過天、按定於東西兩端。恰逢雷神希農穿風而過，讚賞海怪橫天的美色，便拎起他說：「我的追雷獵手正需要這個做弓弦。」隨即把他帶回天屋。賽斯托瓦被囚不安，趁希農忙於指揮風暴時企圖逃脫；但日輪明察，再次把他彎橫天際、塗上最豔的彩繪，好讓希農認出捉回。夏日驟雨之後，紅人望見橫天的絢爛虹彩漸褪、日頭重現，便歡呼：「雨過了！——賽斯托瓦想逃跑，希農又把他押回去了！」

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. A rainbow-from-serpent aition unique in the corpus.

passages.text: In the creation of the earth, which the Turtle bears upon its back, the Sky Woman gave birth to the twins, Hah-gweh-di-yu, and Hah-gweh-da-et-gah; and with their birth, Good and Evil came upon the Earth; for Hah-gweh-da-et-gah was bad minded, and between the brothers there was continual strife. Hah-gweh-di-yu, the Good Minded, was ever striving to create all things beautiful, which angered Hah-gweh-da-et-gah, who sought only to disfigure and destroy. Hah-gweh-di-yu created beautiful rivers, and planted high hills to guard their peaceful flow through the valleys, which enraged Hah-gweh-da-et-gah, who brought forth Sais-tah-go-wa, a sea monster, directing him to enter and destroy them.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 47; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Sais-tah-go-wa, accustomed to the freedom of the broad seas, was furious when restricted by the banks of the streams, and viciously strove to rend them apart, writhing his way through the waters and hurling great rocks upon them as they fled to the sea. Hearing the loss of his rivers should they be engulfed in the deep seas and his high lands and valleys perish from thirst, Hah-gweh-di-yu hastened to their rescue, whereupon, Sais-tah-go-wa, discovering his approach and dreading his power, sought to make his escape, and being unable to return through the rivers he had destroyed, fled to the sky.

title.en: Ska-hai-we, Indian Summer: The Sun Smokes His Peace Pipe
title.zh: 印第安夏：太陽吸起和平之菸

region.en: The south sky where the Sun rests through the winter solstice

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Ska-hai-we, Indian Summer'

summary.en: When in the late autumn the Sun 'walks crooked,' he is on his way to the south sky where during the winter solstice he rests, leaving his sleep spirit on guard during his absence. Previous to his departure he smokes the ah-so-qua-ta (peace pipe) to veil the earth as he councils with the Great Mother. 'Earth, Great Mother, holding your children close to your breast, hear my power! Listen. The days of my glowing are passed. I glare and I burn and I scorch no more. I am lighting my fire from you to kindle my ah-so-qua-ta, the pipe of my sleep. In the haze of my Indian summer I wrap you to silence while Ga-oh holds fast on your pillowing hills the flock of his jealous clouds... Soon I will travel my crooked sky trail. I hurry. I have heard the swift blast of Go-ho-ne's voice... When I sleep in my South, Go-ho-ne is bold, when I open my eyes, Go-ho-ne flies, and He-no grows frightened and still! I am A-deka-ga-gwaa! I reign, and I rule all your lives!... When I come again my warriors will battle throughout the skies; Ga-oh will lock his fierce winds; He-no will soften his voice; Go-ho-ne will fly, and tempests will war no more!'
summary.zh: 深秋時節，太陽「斜行」——那是他趕往南天冬眠的路上，留下「睡靈」代為守夜。臨行前他點燃「阿索誇塔」和平菸斗，以煙靄罩地，與大母親議事。「大母親啊，把你懷中的孩子摟緊，聽我的權能！我發光的時日已盡；我不再灼烤大地。我正從你身上引火，點燃我安眠的菸斗。印第安夏的煙靄把你裹入寧靜，風神在他的雲群中按住你的丘陵……我將沿著斜斜的天路趕路。我聽見冬神戈霍內的疾呼了……我在南方沉睡時，戈霍內便猖狂；我一睜眼，戈霍內便逃，雷神也嚇得啞然！我是太陽阿德卡加瓜！我統御、我掌管你們所有生命！……我再來時，我的戰士將遍戰諸天；風神將鎖住狂風，雷神將柔聲，冬神將奔逃，風暴止息！」

passages.text: When in the late autumn the Sun 'walks crooked,' he is on his way to the south sky where during the winter solstice he rests, leaving his 'sleep spirit' on guard during his absence. Previous to his departure he smokes the ah-so-qua-ta (peace pipe) to veil the earth as he councils with the Great Mother. 'Earth, Great Mother, holding your children close to your breast, hear my power! Listen. The days of my glowing are passed. I glare and I burn and I scorch no more. I am lighting my fire from you to kindle my ah-so-qua-ta, the pipe of my sleep. In the haze of my Indian summer I wrap you to silence while Ga-oh holds fast on your pillowing hills the flock of his jealous clouds. The smoke of my ah-so-qua-ta must not be driven back. Soon I will travel my crooked sky trail. I hurry. I have heard the swift blast of Go-ho-ne's voice, and am flocking the fearing clouds of the Ska-hai-we closer together as they feather the stem of my ah-so-qua-ta.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 48-49; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: 'See! Ga-oh floats gentle winds to the smoke of my ah-so-qua-ta. The north, east, south and west must smoke my peace pipe. I rule the sky! I summon An-da, and she watches my fields. I call Se-oh and she sends forth her stars to guard my dark paths. When He-no, the Thunderer, pours down his rain, I warn as I paint my O-ga-nyo-da to hang on the falling clouds, and He-no hushes his voice... Your mountains will wake when I come again, your mountains will wake, your rivers run fast, and lakes cradle low. Go-ho-ne will flee, I will burn his thongs. Your heart will hear my calling voice. Your seeds will climb to my waiting glow, and your breast flow swift to nourish your young.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 49-50; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: 'Great Mother, listen! I am A-deka-ga-gwaa, the Sun! I rule the skies! I govern An-da. I chase Go-ho-ne. I frighten the shriek of the Thunderer's voice when he furrows my paths with his storms; but when I touch the wings of his flying clouds, they fold the rains fast and sift dews to your thirsting vales. I scorch and I burn, and I kill! I turn my face, and the tempests come. When I sleep in my South, Go-ho-ne is bold, when I open my eyes, Go-ho-ne flies, and He-no grows frightened and still! I am A-deka-ga-gwaa! I reign, and I rule all your lives!... As I sleep down to my dreams, the paths of my sky land slant crooked and small; the breath of my ah-so-qua-ta grows slow, its panting fire dies black, its ashes are pale, the trails grow dark, and my sleep spirit watches near!'
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 50-51; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

region.en: The pathway of spirits (the Milky Way) and the treetops

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Deh-oh-niot, the Evil Soul Gatherer'

summary.en: Sky color is the Deh-oh-niot, who haunts the tall tree tops and the high mountain crests. With the face of a wolf, the wings of a vulture, the body of a panther and claws like a hawk, the Deh-oh-niot wanders in the pathway of spirits - the Milky Way - and is one of the emissaries Death sends to the earth to gather souls. The sick fear him, the dying hear him clawing at the door, where he whines like a cat if the spirit is departing, or barks like a wolf if it is not ready to travel. By the law of Death, Deh-oh-niot can seize only the evil of a spirit which enters his domain; should he capture but a small portion of a soul, he may convey it to Death and be rewarded for his service. If, in a fierce struggle, the spirit should gain its freedom, Deh-oh-niot will have revenge by transforming it into a 'fire stone' and throwing it down to the earth where it may be eternally imprisoned. When a 'fire stone' (meteor) flames through the sky, 'Deh-oh-niot is gathering souls'; and should it fall to the earth, 'Deh-oh-niot has pushed a soul from its trail.' When a comet appears in the heavens, Deh-oh-niot is spreading his tail.
summary.zh: 德奧尼奧特通身天色，出沒於高樹之巔與山峰之脊。牠有狼的面孔、兀鷹的翅膀、豹的身軀與鷹的利爪，遊走於精靈之路——銀河——是死神差往大地收集魂魄的信使之一。病人懼牠，垂死者聽見牠在門外抓撓：魂將離去時牠如貓般哀鳴，魂未就緒時牠如狼般吠叫。依死亡之律，牠只能捕取進入其疆域之魂的惡的部分；即使只攫得魂的一小角，也可上交領賞。若魂在惡鬥中掙脫，牠便化之為「火石」擲回大地，永世囚禁。流星劃空，是「德奧尼奧特在收集魂魄」；流星墜地，是「德奧尼奧特把一個魂推下了它的軌道」；彗星現於天空，是德奧尼奧特在舒展長尾。

passages.text: Sky color is the Deh-oh-niot, who haunts the tall tree tops and the high mountain crests. With the face of a wolf, the wings of a vulture, the body of a panther and claws like a hawk, the Deh-oh-niot wanders in the 'pathway of spirits,' and is one of the emissaries Death sends to the earth to gather souls. The sick fear him, the dying hear him clawing at the door, where he whines like a cat if the spirit is departing, or barks like a wolf if it is not ready to travel.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 51; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: By the law of Death, before whom all departing spirits must pass on their journey, Deh-oh-niot can seize only the evil of a spirit which enters his domain, and even then it may escape him if, in its earth existence, good has predominated. Yet, should Deh-oh-niot be able to capture but a small portion of a soul, he may convey it to Death, and be rewarded for his service. If, in a fierce struggle, the spirit should gain its freedom, Deh-oh-niot will have revenge by transforming it into a 'fire stone,' and throwing it down to the earth where it may be eternally imprisoned. Were Deh-oh-niot any other than sky color, there might be escape from his power; but he can sit on a tree where its top blends with the sky, and there no one can see him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 51-52; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: To hear the voice of Deh-oh-niot is an evil omen, and some dire calamity will follow those who have listened to it. If Deh-oh-niot appears to a person who is not ill, his death will soon follow... When a 'fire stone' (meteor) flames through the sky, 'Deh-oh-niot is gathering souls'; and should it fall to the earth, 'Deh-oh-niot has pushed a soul from its trail.' When a comet appears in the heavens, Deh-oh-niot is spreading his tail.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 52; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Od Je-so-dah and Ji-hen-yah: The Dancing Stars and the Sky Witches

region.en: The Pleiades over the council house at New Year
region.zh: 新年時議屋上空的昂宿

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'Od Je-so-dah and Ji-hen-yah, the Dancing Stars and the Sky Witches'

summary.en: An Indian hunter was teaching his eleven sons the secrets of the forest when, as night shadowed the trees, soft singing voices floated through the stillness till they awakened Hai-no-nis, the eldest. Charmed by the weird chanting, he aroused his brothers to listen, and they followed as it led through bewildering paths to a large tree where under its branches a great circle widened its moon shadows. The song resumed in a quicker strain that tuned them to swift dancing till in the frenzy of its measure they could not cease; delirious with motion, they danced onward and upward till they had left the earth far beneath in their skyward flight. Day after day the brothers danced; the pitying Moon, thinking to quiet them, left her path and led them to her procession of stars, but their ceaseless dancing set the stars whirling till the Moon, frightened at the confusion, transformed them to a group of fixed stars and assigned them the charge of the New Year of the red man, commanding that forevermore they must dance over the council house during the ten days of his New Year's feast. When Hai-no-nis left his brothers he followed the voices - the Ji-hen-yah, the Sky Witches - and promised that if they would not further torment his brothers, they should dance forever in their honor. These Sky Witches frequently descend to the earth in the darkness in search of victims for their sky feasts.
summary.zh: 獵人正教十一個兒子森林的奧秘；夜色籠林之際，柔緩的歌聲飄來，喚醒了長兄海諾尼斯。他被奇異的歌聲迷住，喚醒弟弟們循聲而去，穿過迷離小徑，來到一株大樹下月光圈出的圓地。歌聲再起，節奏轉急，眾兄弟不由自主地旋轉起舞，神志迷離，愈舞愈高，直把大地拋在遙遠的下方。他們晝夜不休地舞著；慈心的月亮離開自己的軌道，領他們加入星辰的行列——但他們不停的舞步把眾星攪得團團轉，月亮驚慌，便把他們化為一群定星，並委以紅人新年的職守：永遠在議屋上空、於新年十日祭期中起舞。海諾尼斯則循聲尋去，發現那是「天巫」吉亨雅；他與她們約定：若不再折磨他的弟弟們，眾星便永遠以舞向他們致敬。這些天巫至今仍常在黑夜降臨大地，為她們的天上盛宴獵取人牲。

sensitivity.note: Converse 1908; public domain. Parker's footnote version: the chief sang the Ji-ha-ya (the witch) song and bade them dance and look upward; one who looked down fell.

passages.text: An Indian hunter was teaching his eleven sons the secrets of the forest, and had led them into its innermost density where game strode unafraid in its stillness... As they slept, soft singing voices floated through the still trees, nearer and nearer approaching till they awakened Hai-no-nis, the eldest of the eleven brothers. Charmed by the weird chanting, he aroused his brothers to listen to the sorcerous song, and they followed as it led through bewildering paths to a large tree where under its branches a great circle widened its moon shadows. For a time the voices ceased, but as the brothers waited, the song was resumed in a quicker strain that tuned them to swift dancing till in the frenzy of its measure, they could not cease. They implored the Night Wind to guide them back to their father, but it passed heedlessly by, and the voices led the brothers still further as, delirious with motion, they danced onward and upward till they had left the earth far beneath in their skyward flight.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 53; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Day after day the brothers danced, and day after day the troubled Sun glanced after them but could not reach them. Night after night the stars grew dizzy as the dancers swirled round the sky, when Hai-no-nis disappeared and the song-voices fainted far away. Yet the dancers could not rest, and the pitying Moon, thinking to quiet them, left her path and led them to her procession of stars which was marching across the night sky. But their ceaseless dancing set the stars whirling till the Moon, frightened at the confusion, transformed them to a group of fixed stars and assigned them the charge of the New Year of the red man, commanding that forevermore they must dance over the council house during the ten days of his New Year's feast.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, pp. 53-54; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: When Hai-no-nis left his brothers he followed the voices, and discovering them to be the Ji-hen-yah (Sky Witches), promised that if they would not further torment his brothers, they should dance forever in their honor. And so the brothers continue to dance, ever obeying the Moon, which sometimes sends them to return wandering stars that may have lost their way in the darkness. These Sky Witches frequently descend to the earth in the darkness in search of victims for their sky feasts which they are ever celebrating. In the astronomical lore of the paleface, this celestial group of dancing brothers is known as the Pleiades, the brilliant constellation in the neck of Taurus.
passages.note: Verbatim from Converse 1908, p. 54; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

region.en: Forest pines whose top branches point east and west
region.zh: 頂枝分指東西的森林高松

source.work: H. M. Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), 'O-so-ah, the Tall Pine, Speaks'

summary.en: The spirit of the pine was once a brave war chief who led his warriors to victory till captured by his enemies and burned at the stake. In the metempsychosis of the Iroquois, the liberated spirit of the chief entered the pine, where it will remain forever the forest guide of the Indian people. It is a fact that the two topmost branches of the pine point to the east and the west, thus furnishing a compass for the red man when lost in the woods. These branches also symbolize the 'deer horns,' the insignia that ranks a chief. The legend relates that the chief of the skyward dancing party hearing the cries of his mother looked down: his act was a fatal one, for he immediately fell like a stone into soft clay, and disappeared. The mother mourned and watched over his grave spot for a year, and when springtime came again she saw a tiny green shoot springing above the sod. When the years passed by, it became a lofty evergreen tree and the people called it O'-so'-a. It was the first of its kind and the soul and blood and body of the chief were in it: this the people knew for they heard it sighing and moaning to its mates in the heavens at night. A thoughtless warrior slashed its bark with his knife and red blood poured out, and it was human blood. 'After many years,' says the story-teller, 'the feathers that dropped from the wide branches sprang up into the pine trees and these have thick sticky blood, but it is good for many things, canoes, ropes and medicines. So it's a good thing he looked down.'
summary.zh: 松樹之靈原是一位勇猛的戰爭酋長，屢戰屢勝，終被敵人所俘，縛上火刑柱燒死。依易洛魁的轉生之說，酋長解脫的魂魄進入了松樹，永為印第安人的林中嚮導。松樹最高的兩根頂枝分指東西，正是紅人迷途時的羅盤；這兩枝也象徵酋長的徽記「鹿角」。傳說說：升天舞隊的首領聽見母親的哭喚而低頭一望，此舉即是死期——他如石墜入軟泥，隨即沒入土中。母親守墓哀哭一年；翌年春天，草土間冒出一莖新綠。歲月流轉，長成參天常綠之樹，人稱「奧索阿」——此樹為其類之首，酋長的魂、血與身皆在其中：人們夜裡聽見它向天上的兄弟嘆息呻吟，便知端的。一個莽撞的戰士以刀割樹皮，樹中流出的竟是人的鮮血。「多年之後，」講故事的人說，「寬枝上落下的羽毛長成了松林，松脂黏稠如血，卻能用來造舟、搓繩、製藥。所以說，他當年低頭一望，倒是件好事。」
